transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Smith. Um, well, I came in because... I drive a taxi, and lately, even when I know for a fact I did my safety check before my shift, this thought just keeps hitting me. Like, out of nowhere, I'll think I missed something on the cab, and because of that, somebody could get hurt, or my boss is going to think I lied about doing the check. And... it's just really bad. I can't make the thought shut up, especially while I'm driving or when I'm trying to study. It just won't stop.

When that thought about missing something on the safety check pops into your head, do you find yourself doing something repeatedly—like going back to re-check the cab, or mentally replaying the checklist over and over—to make the worry go away?

Yeah, exactly. Before I can even take a ride, I end up going around the car over and over again. I'll check the tires, the lights, the doors, the meter, all my paperwork... and I even take pictures of them on my phone sometimes, just to try and prove to myself I did it. 

But if something just doesn't feel right, I have to restart the whole check from the very beginning. I do it even when I have passengers standing there waiting for me and I know I'm already late. I just... I can't drive off until I do it.

latest_inference.note: Patient describes clear obsessions (intrusive fears of causing harm/being blamed) and compulsions (repetitive checking, photographing, restarting rituals) that are time-consuming and distressing, consistent with OCD. This pattern rules out F41.1 (GAD) and F41.9 (unspecified anxiety), which do not typically involve structured compulsive rituals tied to specific obsessions.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports intrusive, unwanted, recurrent thoughts (obsessions) about having missed a safety check, causing significant anxiety and being recognized as excessive/senseless. These thoughts are neutralized by repetitive checking behaviors (compulsions)—re-inspecting the vehicle multiple times, photographing components, and restarting the entire checklist if something 'doesn't feel right.' The compulsions are clearly linked to the obsessive content, are time-consuming, and cause functional impairment (delays, keeping passengers waiting, difficulty concentrating while driving/studying). This symptom pattern—obsessions plus compulsions performed to reduce anxiety, with resultant distress and impairment—is diagnostic of Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (F42) rather than generalized anxiety (no compulsions) or obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (which lacks true intrusive obsessions and ritualized compulsions and instead reflects a pervasive personality trait pattern).
